Values, Morals, Ethics & Law Professional Ethics Ethical Theories Professional bodies and regulations Codes of Conduct for Engineers Guest Lectures - 02 # Case Studies & Discussions PHILOSOPHY OF ETHICS. Ethics is a philosophical discipline of study. It is a systematic approach for understanding, analyzing , and distinguishing matters of right and wrong, good and bad, admirable or deplorable, as they relate to the well-being of all sentient beings. In this section, we would look at the philosophical basics of Ethics. The course unit MN 4900 is focusing on a small branch of the vast subject of Ethics, which is Professional Ethics as applicable for the Engineering profession. Pure Applied VALUES. - personal values - Beliefs of an Individual or a Social Group in which they have an emotional investment (for or against). Values are stable long-lasting beliefs about what is important to a person. They become standards by which people order their lives and make their choices. VALUES, MORALITY, ETHICS & LAW. What you do when no one is looking? Key words of Ethics Intrinsic Values : Truthful, Honest, Loyal, Patient, Goodness, Courage, Forgiving (final destination) Extrinsic Values: Wealth, Physical-fitness, Teamwork (mode to achieve final) VALUES, MORALITY, ETHICS & LAW. Key words of Ethics MORALITY. Values that govern a society's attitude towards right or wrong Examples: -Respect others -Do not judge -Keep your promises -Have courage VALUES, MORALITY, ETHICS & LAW. Key words of Ethics ETHICS. Attempt to develop the means for determining what those values should be Systematic study of Human actions from the point of view of their rightfulness or wrongfulness, as means to attain ultimate happiness Moral principals that govern a person's behavior or conducting of an activity It promotes human welfare or “the good” VALUES. Beliefs of an Individual or a Social Group in which they have an emotional investment (for or against). Values are stable long-lasting beliefs about what is important to a person. They become standards by which people order their lives and make their choices. VALUES, MORALITY, ETHICS & LAW. What you do when no one is looking? Ex: moral, social, economic or political values MORALITY. Values that govern a society's attitude towards right or wrong ETHICS. Attempt to develop the means for determining what those values should be LAW Rules & Regulations enforced by an authority to regulate the conduct of its sujects. Laws are generally based on the moral principles of society. Key words of Ethics ETHICS. The term Ethics derives from the Greek word 'Ethos'. Ethos is the philosophy of RIGHTNESS. and WRONGNESS. of human action. Ethos is a Greek word meaning "character" that is used to describe the guiding beliefs or ideals that characterize a community, nation, or ideology. Key words of Ethics ETHICS. External Rules May vary between environments Influenced by Organization, Grouping, etc. MORALITY MORALITY. is concerned with the Social Practices of what is right and wrong. ETHICS. Right & Wrong Conduct MORALS. Personal Principles Rarely Change Influenced by Culture, Religion, Family, etc. Key words of Ethics Derived from Latin word 'moralitas' which means manner, character, proper behavior. Morally, society says that stealing is wrong. Ethical theory examines and explains why. ETHICS VS MORALS. What does morals mean? A person's idea of morals tends to be shaped their surrounding environment (and sometimes their belief system). Moral values shape a person's ideas about right and wrong. They often provide the guiding ideas behind ethical systems. That's where it gets tricky ... morals are the basis for ethics. A moral person wants to do the right thing, and a moral impulse usually means best intentions. What does ethics mean? Ethics are distinct from morals in that they're much more practical. An ethical code doesn't have to be moral. It's just a set of rules for people to follow. Several professional organizations (like the American Bar Association and the American Medical Association) have created specific ethical codes for their respective fields. In other words, an ethical code has nothing to do with cosmic righteousness or a set of beliefs. It's a set of rules that are drafted by trade groups to ensure members stay out of trouble and act in a way that brings credit to the profession. Key words of Ethics ETHICS VS MORALS. Ethics aren't always moral ... and vice versa It's important to know that what's ethical isn't always what's moral, and vice versa. Omerta, is a code of silence among members of the Mafia. It was used to protect criminals from the police. This follows the rules of ethically-correct behavior for the organization, but it can also be viewed as wrong from a moral standpoint. A moral action can also be unethical. A lawyer who tells the court that his client is guilty may be acting out of a moral desire to see justice done, but this is deeply unethical because it violates the attorney-client privilege. Key words of Ethics ETHICS VS MORALS. Generally, the terms ethics and morality are used interchangeably, although a few different communities (academic, legal, or religious, for example) will occasionally make a distinction. Both morality and ethics loosely have to do with distinguishing the difference between “good and bad” or “right and wrong.” Ref: https://www.britannica.com/story/whats-the-difference-between-morality-and-ethics Many people think of morality as something that's personal and normative, whereas ethics the standards of “good and bad” distinguished by a certain community or social setting. For example, your local community may think adultery is immoral, and you personally may agree with that. However, the distinction can be useful if your local community has no strong feelings about adultery, but you consider adultery immoral on a personal level. By these definitions of the terms, your morality would contradict the ethics of your community. In popular discourse, however, we'll often use the terms moral and immoral when talking about issues like adultery regardless of whether it's being discussed in a personal or in a community-based situation. As you can see, the distinction can get a bit tricky. Key words of Ethics ETHICS MORALS. Key words of Ethics EASTERN VS WESTERN ETHICS. Cowboy vs Ninja / Samurai Ethics What is it? Both examined human nature and what is needed for people to move toward well-being. • Differences: the western ethics is generally for people to achieve self-direction and to understand themselves personally. • The eastern ethics often is to understand universal interconnections, to be liberated from the self. Although, eastern ethics is not imposed from outside of a person but is instead imposed from within oneself. Morals Principles or habits with respect to ,right or wrong conduct. Hinduism, Buddhism, etc. Roman, Christian etc. APPROACH. Holistic and Cultural Rational CONFLICT & HARMONY. Good & Bad, Light & Dark all exist in equilibrium Good must triumph over Evil PROFESSIONAL ETHICS. Professional ethics are principles that govern the behaviour of a person or group in a business environment. The difference between personal and professional ethics: Personal Ethics - Refers to the ethics that a person identifies with in respect to people and situations that they deal with in everyday life. Professional Ethics - Refers to the ethics that a person must adhere to in respect of their interactions and business dealings in their professional life. In some cases, personal and professional ethics may clash and cause a moral conflict. For example: A police officer may personally believe that a law that he is required to enforce is wrong. However, under the Code of Conduct for the Police, he is required to obey all lawful and reasonable instructions to enforce that law unless there is good and sufficient cause to do otherwise. A doctor may not personally believe that the course of medical treatment chosen by a patient is the right one. However, under the Code of Ethics for the Medical Association, he/she must respect the rights, autonomy and freedom of choice of the patient. WHY STUDY PROFESSIONAL ETHICS. Knowledge of Professional Ethics will provide following desirable balanced outcomes for Engineers: b) Increased knowledge of relevant standards of conduct c) Improved ethical judgment a) Increased ethical sensitivity and d) Improved ethical will-power (greater ability to act ethically when required) SENSITIVE STANDARDS JUDGEMENT WILL POWER WHY STUDY PROFESSIONAL ETHICS SENSITIVE STANDARDS JUDGEMENT WILL POWER.  People rely heavily on engineers to provide them with safe and reliable goods and services. Engineers must perform under a certain standard of professional behavior which requires adherence to the highest principles of ethical conduct. Mistakes made by unethical and/or incompetent engineers do not just cost money, they could cost many lives WHY STUDY PROFESSIONAL ETHICS SENSITIVE STANDARDS JUDGEMENT WILL POWER. Ethics is a systematic approach for understanding, analyzing , and distinguishing matters of right and wrong, good and bad, admirable or deplorable, as they relate to the well-being of all sentient beings. The course unit MN 4900 is focusing on a small branch of the vast subject of Ethics, which is Professional Ethics as applicable for the Engineering profession. Pure Applied Applied Ethics A quick recap Profession A profession is a type of job that requires advanced education & training. Profession is: • A group of individuals sharing the same occupation organized to work in an ethically permissible way. • Members of a profession set and follow special standards for carrying on their occupational work. At its core, it's meant to be an indicator of trust and expertise. Attributes of a Profession Attributes of a profession include: Work that requires sophisticated skills, the use of intellectual judgment, and the exercise of discretion & Work that is not routine and cannot be mechanized. Membership in the profession requires extensive recognized formal education, not simply practical training or apprenticeship. The public allows special societies, institutes or organizations that are controlled by members of the profession to set standards for admission to the profession, to set standards of conduct for members, and to enforce these standards. Significant public-good results from the practice of the profession. Most professions tend to be relatively well compensated. Who is a Professional ? A professional is a person who carries out a specialized type of job that needs a high level of education and training in the specific domain. • Member of a professional group • Sees other members, including those employed elsewhere, as peers/colleagues • Exercises judgment in the performance of occupational tasks and follows relevant professional standards. • Accepts the profession's agreement to work in an ethically permissible way (code of ethics) Engineer Accountant Doctor Lawyer Investment Banker Teacher Sportsman Nurse Mechanic Dentist Electrician Programmer Pharmacist Chef Professional Ethics වෘත්තීය ආචාරධරේm ெதாழில்«ைற ெநறி«ைறகள் Toḻilmuṟai neṟimuṟaikaḷ Professional Ethics are principles that govern the behaviour of a person or group in a business environment. Professional Ethics are: • Often codified as a set of rules / code • All those in a particular group will follow the same code Like values, professional ethics provide rules on how a person should act towards other people and institutions in such an environment. Professional Values Your professional values are the core values and ethics you adopt and demonstrate in the workplace. These traits include skills, behaviors and actions that many employers look for and desire in an employee. There are several professional values, Accountability Responsibility Integrity Professional Attitude Continuous Learning Team work Accountability • Accountability is considered as the key professional value that any employee must hold onto. An employee needs to take responsibility his actions. If you are a leader, you are accountable for the actions of your team also. game is an integral part of any organization but you must try to change the trend and accept the results of your actions. Responsibility • Most of the people get confused between accountability & responsibility. However, both of them are quite different. While you are accountable for the results of your action, it is your responsibility to perform those actions to take out the results. An employee needs to be responsible for the duties assigned to him. Following the rules and regulations of the company and diligently performing your duties make you a responsible employee. Integrity • Accept what you do; good or bad. Never take credit the work done by others. This is somehow a fine example of a and professional trait that is a must in an employee. Be honest and true to the company. Professional Attitude • This is a must aspect. You need to be positive and motivated. If you are a leader, your positivity must inspire others. You must accept the feedbacks regarding you in a positive manner & should always be open to communication. An employee must know how to handle pressure and stress in adverse conditions. Continuous Learning • Another trait that ensures your career growth is having a continuous learning approach. An employee has to learn from every opportunity provided. Accept what you do not know and try to learn it from others. Team Work • To become successful, you need to do teamwork & one day you may definitely be the leader of a team. Taking the complete team together is an important value for a team leader. You must ensure that all the team members are on the same page. Professional Ethics • Professional ethics is guidance for people working in a particular profession that tells them what they supposed to do and what they are not supposed to do while working there. Engineering Ethics. Engineering Ethics is the field of applied ethics which Examines and Sets Standards for Engineers' obligations to the public, clients, employers and the profession and is appropriate in all aspects of professional practice. Engineers may face Ethical Issues with technical practice, and with broader business conduct. Ethical Issues faced by Engineers: Relationships with clients, consultants, competitors, and contractors Ensuring legal compliance by clients, client's contractors, and others Conflict of interest Bribery and kickbacks, which might include: Gifts, meals, services, entertainment and recreation opportunities Treatment of confidential or proprietary information Consideration of the employer's assets Outside employment / activities (moonlighting) TECHNICAL BUSINESS. Applied Ethics Appropriate Professional Practice Engineering Ethics SETS STANDARDS. Public Clients Employers Profession Why study Engineering Ethics? SENSITIVE STANDARDS JUDGEMENT WILL POWER.  People rely heavily on Engineers to provide them with Safe and Reliable goods, services and built environments. Engineers must perform under a certain standard of professional behavior which requires adherence to the highest principles of ethical conduct. Mistakes made by unethical and/or incompetent Engineers do not just cost money, they could cost many lives A quick recap Ethical Dilemmas in Engineering Notes for CAUTION:. Some may tend to mis-use the definitions of Engineering Ethics to sabotage or mis-represent facts due to their inability to come to rational conclusions based on given constraints or due to Egoistic, non-corporative behaviours. At the end, Engineers have to be practical in achieving the goals without compromising any principles of Engineering or Professional Ethics. Engineers provide practical solutions with given constrains of available resources, technology and skills. Engineers are key decision makers in most business environments Managers, Consultants, Project Managers, Design Engineers, Implementors, etc. They will always face Ethical challenges or DILEMMAs which demands for clear knowledge and skills of ethics for decision making. Principles of Engineering Ethics The engineers have a great role to play in the betterment of society. Following fundamental principles of engineering are the guiding codes that every engineer must follow in order to function in an ethical manner. Respect for Law, Public Good, and Life - The wider public interest must be the sole concentration of the engineer; he or she must respect the law of the land and practice their professions within the boundaries of the law. The engineer should be aware of the scarcity of both natural resources and humans. The engineering ethics essay is lengthy and time- consuming; we provide both engineering ethics essay and assignment help at a very nominal price. Come reap the benefit of our services. Accuracy and Rigor - It is essential that the engineers use their knowledge and skill for the service of society and its betterment. They must perform their duty with care and competence; the skills should be updated according to the developing trends in the industry; not mislead others and get misled on the matters of engineering. Integrity and Honesty - It is the responsibility of every engineer to be fair, honest, and demonstrate professional conduct. It is also the responsibility of the engineer to take care that their works don't harm the other party, be honest and non- deceptive, avoid corrupt practices, rejection of bribery, etc. Responsible Leadership - An engineer should be a responsible and coherent leader in the field he or she may be operating. The leader should be aware of the new technology and the concerns of the society; promote the achievements of engineering; the statements made in a professional capacity must be truthful. The following case is based on a recorded case from the NSPE knowledge base extracted with consent. Plaintiff Accused • Client-Y (Occupant of Building) Lawyer-X Engineer-A (consultant) • Owner of Building • Building material manufacturers Background : Lawsuit in connection with a building fire that resulted in the death and injury of several individuals Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION ENGINEER'S DILEMMA: ??. Engineer-A is employed by Lawyer-X to conduct a forensic engineering investigation Engineer provides investigation report The investigation reveals safety standards issues in the Building Materials used in the build After the Engineer's report, Lawyer-X and Client-Y enter into a private settlement with the accused Approved by the court Under the terms of the settlement, Engineer-A is ordered not to reveal the contents of forensic engineering report Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION ENGINEER'S DILEMMA:. Engineer-A is concerned that the settlement will undermine her obligation to the public, because she believes the forensic engineering report contains important findings relating to the use of manufactured building materials. QUESTION:. What are Engineer-A's obligations under the circumstances? Confidentiality Obligation to Public Codes of Ethics - Compared IESL - Basic Principles Public Goodness is Paramount Uphold Professional dignity 3 Practice Sustainable engineering Build Reputation on Merit 5 Limit to area of competence 6 Serve benefactors faithfully with no conflict to other principles Speak out objectively & truthfully 8 Continuously develop knowledge and skills NSPE - Fundamental Canons Hold Paramount the Safety, Health & Welfare of the Public Perform services only in the areas of competence 3 Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees 5 Avoid deceptive acts Conduct honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully so as to enhance the honor, reputation, and usefulness of the profession Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION. Conflicts between fundamental provisions of Code of Ethics are common. Among such conflicts are situations in which the public interest and the protection of the public health and safety are matched against ethical duties of confidentiality to clients. Both values are vital to engineering ethics and professionalism and need to be maintained in order to protect the integrity of the engineering profession. Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION NSPE. Code of Ethics References IESL Code Equivalent Applicable Codes of Ethics: 1 - Health, safety and welfare of the public is paramount ... 1.5 - In the event of their judgment being over- ruled in matters pertaining to health, safety and welfare of the community, inform their clients or employers ..... to inform the relevant authority. 1.7 - Alert authorities on violation of code .... Section II.1.a. - If engineers' judgment is overruled under circumstances that endanger life or property, they shall notify their employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate. Section II.1. - Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION NSPE. Code of Ethics References IESL Code Equivalent 1.6 - Shall contribute to public discussion ... for the well being of the community .... 5.7 - Shall neither disclose nor use confidential information gained in the course of their employment without express permission, except where public interest and safety are involved. Section III.2.a. - Engineers are encouraged to participate in civic affairs; career guidance for youths; and work for the advancement of the safety, health, and well-being of their community. Section III.4. - Engineers shall not disclose, without consent, confidential information concerning the business affairs or technical processes of any present or former client or employer, or public body on which they serve. Continued Applicable Codes of Ethics: Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION. Analysis: The facts in the present case relate not to a written confidentiality agreement, but instead to a court-approved settlement agreement requiring confidentiality. Also, the facts of this case do not suggest Engineer A's technical concerns involved matters of urgency or imminent harm to the public health and safety. Confidentiality Obligation to Public Engineering Ethics - Case Studies Case1: CONFIDENTIALITY - FIRE INVESTIGATION. Conclusion: • Engineer A has an ethical obligation to maintain the confidentiality of the forensic engineering report. • Engineer A may also explore an alternative path to identify the technical issues involved, such as further research that explains her technical concerns without revealing specific and identifiable facts and circumstances that would compromise the settlement agreement involving Client Y. This approach would be a reasonable middle ground for Engineer A to pursue and which would fulfill her ethical responsibilities both to the public and to the client. Defensible Decisions Vs Correct Decisions * When faced with an Ethical Dilemmas both possible outcomes may have some good and some bad * Hence there may be no CORRECT DECISION. ¢ What we would strive for is a DEFENSIBLE DECISION. A defensible decision is based upon sound reasoning and can be DEFENDED. in any forum ¢ The objective of sound ethical decision making is to make Defensible Decisions Approaches to Ethical decision making * Quick tests provided through the informal tests - eg TV test ° Fundamental decision making using Ethical Frameworks ¢ Pre-canned guidelines provided through Codes of Ethics / Conduct Informal Guidelines in Ethical Decision Making Informal Tests help in supporting quick ethical decisions ¢ Moral Intution Test - First Impressions - First impression or Reaction ¢ Shushers Test - Don't tell anyone lf we do an action but want it hushed the chances are that it is something unethical - eg “We are releasing the buggy software but Sh!! Don't tell anyone.” ¢ Mom Test - Would u tell Mom? | donot want my Mum to know about something | did, Chances are that it is something unethical. Informal Guidelines in Ethical Decision Making (Cont) TV Test - Would u tell on TV? lf we release a great new software we may want to talk about it on TV. Will this action add to enhancing my personal brand or not? Smell Test= Does situ smell? - Does the situation small bad? Eg - trying to do something behind one's back may not smell right !! Other persons shoe Test - Reverse Roles? Formal Ethical Theories Formal Ethfeal Theories * Consequentialist Theory (Teleologist Theory) Focus is on the consequences of the action - Hedonism * Egoistic - What is best for me ¢ Universal - What is best for others Not much used in Ethical Decision Making - Utilitarian - What gives Happiness for greater No Widely used in Ethical Decision Making Formal Ethical Theories ¢ Deontologist Theory - Based Rights and Duties of Stakeholders - Eg Human Rights, Animal Rights, Children's Rights ¢ Aright often has an associated duty - What Rights are violated? - What Duties are neglected? Formal Ethical Theories ¢ Virtue Ethics - - What would a virtuous person do in this case? ¢ Kant's Imperative - 2 formulations Kant's Categorical Imperative (15t Formulation) Act only from moral rules that you can at the same time will to be universal moral laws. Proposed rule: “| may make promises with the intention of later breaking them.” The person in trouble Fe his promise to be believed so he can get what he needs. Universalize rule: Everyone may make & break promises Everyone breaking promises would make promises unbelievable, contradicting desire to have promise believed The rule is flawed. The answer is “No.” Illustration of 1%: Formulation Question: Can | drive through the red light at a road crossing if it does not obstruct or endanger anyone Proposed rule: “| may break rules as long as it does not hurt any one” Universalize rule: Everyone may break rules as long a it does not hurt anyone Lecture 02 Everyone breaking rules may lead to a chaotic situation The rule is flawed. The answer is “No.” Categorical Imperative (2°? Formulation) Act so that you treat both yourself and other people as ends in themselves and never only as a means to an end. Enter Room? - Knowledge about a person - Do you have a girl / boy friend? Privacy is a Human Right - violations challenge human dignity Benefits @f Privacy ¢ Individual growth ¢ Individual responsibility ¢ Freedom to be yourself Intellectual and spiritual growth ¢ Development of loving, trusting, caring, intimate relationships Harms of Privacy * Cover for illegal /immoral / anti social activities e May prevent help getting to people with psychiatric issues / dysfunctional families / those who do not talk about their problems ¢ Can trigger loneliness Information Technology Erodes Privacy j ¢ Information collection, exchange, combination, and distribution easier than ever means less privacy ¢ Today we leave an “electronic trail” of information behind us and others can do many things with this info Public Records Public record: Held by government agencies Examples: birth certificates, marriage certificates, NIC information, motor vehicle records, criminal records, deeds to property, electors lists, Tax records, Exam Results Computerized databases and Internet have made public records much easier to access - Eg: Electors lists available through the internet, Exam results released on Internet Right to Information and Privacy The RTI act obliges government to disclose certain information when such information is formally requested by the public under the RTI act However such disclosures could sometimes infringe on someone's privacy - eg Requesting salary information of state employees We need to balance the public good against the right to privacy - see https://www.colombotelegraph.com/index.php/srilank an-airlines-trade-unions-protest-following-rti-release- of-salary-details-of-ceo-and-others/ Confidentiality ¢ Confidentiality refers to the data that is captured ¢ Once captured, the data should be kept confidential ¢ Data should only be shared on a need to know basis ¢ Proper security should be exercised at all times Privacy Guidelines ¢ Consider the privacy issues surrounding the data being captured - eg CCTV recordings/ Voice recordings - Keep the subjects informed of purpose / Get consent ¢ Collect only data that is required - no more Confidentiality / Data Protection Guidelines Handle data in a responsible way Employ proper data security procedures Keep data only as long as it is required - destroy data responsibly If no longer needed Use data for the purpose it was collected. Data captured for one purpose should not be used for another purpose without the permission of the subject - Using conference registration data for product promotions Share data only with those who need to know When using data for analysis anonymize the data so that ownership cannot be traced Lecture Legal Framework Some countries have provided a formal legal framework to ensure protection of data held in computers or filings - Eg UK Data Protection Act 1998 Sri Lanka enacted the Personal Data Protection Act No 9 of 2022 in March 2022 Provisions also exist for data protection in certain sectors is provided in specific acts - Eg: Banking Act, Telecom Act, Registration of Persons Act GDPR ¢ The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) is a regulation by which the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European Commission intend to strengthen and unify data protection for all individuals within the European Union (EU). ¢ Came into operation in March 2018
